newsitem.title: UK: Subdued UK industry data will help Clarke on rates.
newsitem.headline: Subdued UK industry data will help Clarke on rates.

text.p: A sober set of manufacturing output data for December on Thursday will aid Britain's Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke in his bid not to tighten monetary policy before the next election, economists said.
While output picked up in the last month of 1996 after a shock downturn in November, analysts said growth rates were still weak and constituted no threat to interest rates for now.
"These figures provide confirmation that while the manufacturing recovery remains on track, it is still fragile," said Jonathan Loynes, UK economist at HSBC in London.
"Clarke has ample justification for leaving interest rates unchanged this side of the general election."
Manufacturing output rose 0.2 percent on the month in December after a decline of 0.3 percent in November, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said.
Analysts had forecast a 0.3 percent gain for December.

Clarke, who left base rates steady after his meeting with Bank of England Governor Eddie George on Wednesday, is anxious to keep monetary policy on hold before the country votes in an election due by May 22.
"These data are soft enough to allow the Chancellor to maintain a steady rate policy in the near term at least," said Jeremy Hawkins at Bank of America.
"The odds are still very much in favour of no rate hike this side of the election."

Analysts said the weaker than expected industry data reinforced the view that Britain's economic pick-up was very much consumer-driven, with exports -- under pressure from a recent spirited rise in sterling -- playing second fiddle.
"There is no doubt that this has become a consumer-led recovery, as opposed to the export-led recovery of a year or two ago," said Robin Marshall, chief economist at Chase in London.
As the year goes on, rising spending capacity across the nation will begin to boost the services sector, feeding though into stronger industrial production further down the line, economists said.
"Inventories are now lean... so if dometic demand picks up as anticipated, output should similarly accelerate over the coming months," said Hawkins.
But the increase would have to be quite significant before Eddie George's argument for higher interest rates would find any sound basis in production figures.

Angela Knight, Economic Secretary to the Treasury, said Thursday's data showed the "wheel and cogs of manufacturing turning faster" in the second half of 1996, adding that recent surveys suggested that higher production was on the way in 1997.

The latest Confederation of British Industry (CBI) survey showed manufacturing output grew steadily over the past four months, but it also said sterling's strength may be starting to erode demand for exports.
Analysts said the strength of the pound was likely to keep output down for a while to come.
Simon Briscoe, economist at Nikko in London, said he saw little chance of output gaining pace on a month-on-month basis in the next few months.
"The strength of the pound since the summer will increasingly hamper the competitiveness of UK exporters, feeding through to the data over the next six months or so," he said.
"The message continues to be one of painfully slow expansion."
